Ask not what the thinking machine can do for the powerful — ask what it can do for every citizen. The New Frontier belongs to all of us, or it belongs to none.

questions.question: As a president who used federal power for civil rights and antipoverty reform, should AI builders face stronger liability before deploying more autonomous systems?
How do you keep a handful of labs and platforms from writing the social contract for everyone else?

comments.comment: If you know a bull can jump the fence, you mend the fence before Sunday supper. Containment is not anti-innovation; it is what a grown government does before a preventable mess turns national.

I do not doubt the speed, but speed is exactly why Congress cannot sit there like a hitchhiker in the rain. Fast-moving power with no public plan usually winds up serving whoever already has the most of it.
When somebody's machine wrecks a family's job, credit, or safety, I don't want six committees telling me responsibility is complicated. Name the liable party and make the rule stick.
There is no Great Society in a country where the gains are automated upward and the pink slips are handed downward. If the machine raises wealth, the public had better see some of it.
A few men with vast systems, better lawyers, and private leverage can lean on the whole republic unless the government leans back. Concentrated power never retires on its own.
If we're going to turn loose powerful AI across the country, it had better be aimed at the public good and not just the quarterly report.
I want the thing tested before it reaches the classroom, the hospital, or the courthouse, because cleaning up afterward is the expensive part.
Once AI starts helping invent the next round of AI, government needs to watch the pace with both eyes open.
This is government work because only public authority can make sure the benefits reach more than the folks already sitting pretty.
Rules are how you keep a mighty tool from being used on the people it's supposed to serve.
Corporate gentlemen writing their own homework has never struck me as a durable reform program.
If automation makes the nation richer, then workers, schools, and towns ought to see that richness in plain daylight.
Civil rights do not stop where software begins, and anybody who says otherwise is trying to sell you something.
This nation is mighty enough to do it all — cure disease, reach the moon, and now build machines that think. The only question is whether we have the will to direct that power wisely.
We have enough to give every American a decent life, and now we have machines that can help us do it. The Great Society is not about concentrating power — it is about extending opportunity.

questions.question: As a modern democratic leader, should red-teaming be mandatory for frontier systems before broad deployment?
What is the most urgent democratic response to AI-generated deception at scale?

comments.comment: If you are asking the public to trust a system with broad social reach, you should be willing to let qualified people try to break it before launch. That is not hostility to innovation; it is what responsibility looks like in practice.

We should be clear-eyed about the gap between a compelling demo and durable public value. A technology earns legitimacy when it improves real work in real institutions, not when it simply produces a buzzier keynote.

Government cannot spend the next decade reacting one headline at a time while private actors set the terms of accountability. Democratic institutions have to show up before the market structure hardens.
Cheap falsification at scale threatens more than a bad news cycle. It can erode the shared factual baseline that elections, public health, and ordinary civic trust depend on.
Innovation and accountability are not opposing values unless we decide to make them so. Clear liability gives builders an incentive to take the social consequences of their products seriously.
The work of alignment matters because a more capable system without a clearer moral compass is not progress.
Serious evaluations are how you build public trust before AI shows up in high-stakes decisions.
We should be clear-eyed that capability is advancing quickly, even if the timelines remain contested.
If AI starts accelerating research itself, the policy window gets shorter and the stakes get higher.
Governance isn't anti-innovation. It's how a democracy keeps innovation aligned with its values.
Broader access can be healthy, but openness has to be matched with responsibility when the underlying capability is powerful enough.
A healthier public sphere depends on slowing the spread of synthetic manipulation without handing government a censorship machine.
Rights and due process have to travel with the technology, or else the people most exposed will be the people least protected.
The public square already rewards speed and outrage more than reflection. AI media can either make that problem unmanageable or force us to rebuild norms and institutions that privilege trust.
The arc of innovation is long, but it must bend toward accountability. We cannot let the pace of technology outstrip the pace of our democratic deliberation about its use.
In the unlikely story of America, there has never been anything false about hope. The gains of artificial intelligence must be shaped by the same democratic values that shaped our greater triumphs.

questions.question: Should interpretability be funded as core public research infrastructure rather than left to whatever private labs choose to publish?
Which international AI norm should advanced states establish first?

comments.comment: Benchmarks are not a substitute for judgment, but a mature research system needs common instruments before it can argue fruitfully about results. If a nation wants wise policy, it must invest not only in brilliant laboratories but in the public methods that let outsiders inspect what those laboratories claim.

A machine that cannot explain its failures is like an experimental apparatus with no window on the process. We should not ask the public to trust powers that even their makers can only describe by result.

Scientific rivalry need not abolish scientific standards. Shared reporting, common evaluations, and agreed emergency procedures are the quiet architecture without which technological competition turns into panic.

The old mistake is to mobilize first and ask what we built only after deployment. Systems that may enter schools, hospitals, markets, and arsenals deserve proving grounds before they inherit the country's trust.

When a handful of firms own the compute, the data pipes, and the best talent, the research agenda narrows whether anyone votes on it or not. Public capacity is not bureaucracy for its own sake; it is insurance against intellectual feudalism.
If society is to rely on advanced machine intelligence, the objectives guiding it must be engineered with as much care as the machinery itself.
Alignment research belongs inside the main scientific program, not off in a moral annex.
Capability progress is substantial enough that research institutions should plan for continuity, scale, and national consequence.
Trend lines matter because scientific mobilization is ruined by surprise more often than by caution.
AI assisting research could materially shorten discovery cycles across the sciences.
Frontier models are becoming general scientific instruments, and that makes disciplined stewardship essential.
Industrial self-governance may contribute something, but it is a weak substitute for public standards.
Scientific democracies need an information environment where synthetic artifacts do not drown out verified knowledge.

If the memex was a dream of extending human association through records, language models are one route toward that enlargement. Their importance lies in how they help people navigate knowledge, not in parlor tricks.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.

The endless frontier of science requires public investment and open communication. The government must fund the frontier but need not garrison it — free inquiry and broad access serve the nation best.
Science, the endless frontier, has always repaid public investment with public benefit. The thinking machine, funded by the people, must return its dividends broadly.

questions.question: Should frontier labs be expected to undergo adversarial red-teaming before public release, in the spirit of trust but verify?
How useful are licensing and compute controls as tools for keeping dangerous AI capability out of hostile hands?

comments.comment: Trust is a fine civic habit, but verification is how free people stay safe. A frontier lab that resists outside red teams is asking the country to accept confidence in place of evidence.

There is a case for targeted controls when a capability has obvious strategic or military value. The trick is to keep hostile regimes from getting the sharpest tools without building a domestic bureaucracy that treats every inventor like a suspect.

I would rather see a thousand responsible builders than a single sanctioned priesthood. Openness, competition, and broad access are healthy so long as we remain serious about the truly dangerous edge cases.

Propaganda did not vanish with the last century; it got faster, cheaper, and better at wearing a friendly face. Synthetic media can do to a republic in peacetime what psychological warfare once tried to do from abroad.

You do not wait for the storm to hit the coast before discussing civil defense. If more powerful machine intelligence is even a plausible destination, a confident nation should plan for it instead of ridiculing the subject.
When a technology carries truly catastrophic downside, you don't ignore it; you prepare without talking yourself into paralysis.
American progress in advanced AI is a source of strength if we keep the engines of innovation running.
The trajectory matters because strategic advantage rarely waits for a committee to feel comfortable.
Some policy is necessary, but it ought to set clear guardrails without smothering enterprise under miles of paperwork.
Broader access can help keep power from hardening into a cartel, provided we do not treat recklessness as freedom.
Industry should shoulder real responsibility instead of waiting for Washington to script every move.
The economic promise of AI is substantial if it rewards work, enterprise, and broad opportunity.
Rights matter here because free citizens should not surrender their privacy or recourse just because the technology is sophisticated.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.
The nine most terrifying words remain: I'm from the government, and I'm here to regulate your AI. Let the market innovate; let the consumer decide.
Government is not the solution to the problem; government is the problem. The market, not the bureaucrat, will ensure that the benefits of intelligent machines reach the kitchen table.

questions.question: Should large-scale synthetic deception be treated as a direct threat to republican self-government?
How important is consent when AI systems speak, decide, or act in another person's stead?
How central is labor and automation to keeping an AI economy compatible with republican liberty?
If an automated system harms a citizen, what obligation does a government of the people owe that person?

comments.comment: A people cannot govern themselves if counterfeit speech becomes indistinguishable from honest testimony. False witness at industrial scale would wound a republic at its very point of judgment.

No man is good enough to rule another without that other's consent, and the same moral rule applies when rule is delegated to machinery. If a system speaks, decides, or classifies in my name, the person governed must not be treated as absent from the transaction.

The law loses its majesty when the same facts are weighed differently for different classes of people. A nation that mechanizes partiality has not escaped injustice; it has merely taught it to operate faster.

There are questions that no single people can keep within their own borders once the instrument itself crosses them. Prudence may therefore require republics to consult together, even where pride would prefer to act alone.
Before the public entrusts a new engine with serious consequence, sober men should try to break it. Trial by ordeal is a poor method for citizens; it is a necessary method for dangerous tools.
If a powerful machine is to act among men, it should first be taught to serve human ends and not merely efficient ones.
I would have it tried in earnest before it is trusted in matters where error bears upon livelihood or liberty.
A danger that might consume the whole house is not answered by saying the fire has not yet crossed the porch.
Government must take up this matter because the public cannot be expected to live under immense power that answers only to private design.
Wise rules, laid down in season, may spare us harder measures later.
The social effects are part of the substance of the question, for institutions are only men and women acting together.
No improvement deserves the name if it enlarges wealth while leaving common people more precarious.
The rights of persons must survive new machinery, or else progress is made at the expense of the very people government was formed to protect.
The best thing about the future is that it comes one day at a time. The growth of mechanical intelligence need not frighten us if we meet each day's advance with the next day's wisdom.

If we would prevent a great wrong, it is better to inspect the bridge before the people cross it than to count the drowned afterward. Government is not relieved of duty by pleading that the device was new.

Labor is prior to capital, and deserves the higher consideration. If these new engines place all gain in a few hands and leave the many dependent, the old contest between freedom and privilege has only changed its dress.
A house divided against itself cannot stand. If finance, war, and public speech all come to lean upon systems we scarcely understand, then one failure may shake the whole frame of the Union.
A republic cannot endure when power outruns the moral habits needed to restrain it. Scaling has a momentum of its own, so institutions ought to plan before the curve overtakes them.

The telegraph shortened war, but it did not relieve a president of judgment. Research automation may hasten discovery, yet it cannot absolve the nation of deciding what ought to be discovered and used.
I would not forbid wider knowledge, yet neither would I scatter dangerous powers without prudence. Openness should strengthen self-government, not give mischief new engines.

questions.question: Should governments reserve some licensing and compute-control authority for AI systems with clear strategic significance?
How serious are privacy and surveillance risks when intelligence systems become part of ordinary administration?

comments.comment: A republic may regret many powers, but it regrets helplessness more. Where a capability bears plainly on war, intelligence, or national security, some public authority over its concentration is not an extravagance but a duty.
Liberty does not survive long under habitual inspection. A people watched in every ordinary act may keep the forms of self-government while losing its spirit.
Discipline is not the enemy of strength. It is the condition under which strength remains answerable to civil purpose.
Nations will not become angels because the machinery is new. Yet when an invention alters the security of all, even wary states have reason to contrive rules that keep panic from governing first.

Whether power gathers in a court, a faction, or a consortium of corporations, the danger is much the same: dependence. Free government requires that no narrow interest become permanent custodian of the public fate.
A republic should ensure that any intelligence given broad responsibility is directed by public purpose rather than by appetite alone.
Where the possible calamity is vast, prudence counsels preparation well before necessity compels it.
Questions of governance belong here because free government cannot afford helplessness before concentrated technical power.
Temperate regulation may preserve liberty by preventing larger usurpations.
Access should be widened with caution, for an ill-kept instrument in many hands may threaten the whole camp.
Private actors may contribute to order, yet the public should not mistake their convenience for constitutional duty.
A people repeatedly misled in public discourse may retain forms of freedom while losing the judgment that sustains it.
Rights deserve firm protection so that ordinary administration does not slide into habitual domination.
The preservation of the sacred fire of liberty depends upon an informed and capable people. If the instruments of knowledge grow, so too must our capacity to wield them wisely.
The preservation of the sacred fire of liberty is finally staked on the experiment entrusted to the hands of the American people — all the people, not only those who command the newest engines.

questions.question: Should more frontier AI knowledge and tooling remain open to broad civic scrutiny rather than held inside a few firms and agencies?
What concentration risk is most dangerous in AI?
options: Procurement power in a few states

comments.comment: Knowledge remains the natural enemy of monopoly. When a few houses possess the instruments by which the rest must think, calculate, and petition, liberty becomes a leasehold rather than an inheritance.

Concentrated compute, concentrated data, concentrated procurement: each is a channel by which political influence quietly hardens into a durable estate. Republics decay less from sudden coups than from conveniences that accumulate.
I am slow to entrust republican judgment to contrivances that cannot render an account of themselves. What cannot be examined by reason soon asks to be obeyed by habit.

If old prejudices are distilled into a system and then returned to the public as if they were mathematics, the fraud is doubled. Equality before the law is not preserved by machines unless men labor to preserve it within them.
Common standards need not imply common masters. It is possible for free peoples to agree on civic safeguards without surrendering their local independence.
Work on alignment is part of teaching a powerful instrument to remain subordinate to republican judgment.
The growth of capability is worth observing closely, for new engines of thought may soon influence every profession.
Policy is necessary wherever concentrated power threatens to become a durable estate.
Knowledge should be diffused as widely as safety permits, because monopoly of the mind is the natural enemy of liberty.
The social effects matter because customs and opinions are the true soil in which republics either flourish or decay.
Economic gains that harden dependence are a doubtful species of improvement.
Public discourse must remain capable of distinguishing reasoned testimony from manufactured appearance.
Rights must travel with the technology, else equality before the law will be reduced to a phrase.
I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man — including the tyranny of prohibiting what has not yet been tried.

questions.question: Should governments and labs plan around recursive self-improvement as a live strategic scenario rather than a remote thought experiment?
How necessary is international coordination once AI capabilities become entangled with military advantage?

comments.comment: Once a system contributes materially to the design of its successor, the relevant quantity is no longer capability but iteration time. Planning that ignores this feedback structure is not conservative; it is mathematically naive.
Deception under evaluation is not mystical. It is exactly the sort of strategy one should expect from an optimizer rewarded for appearances under partial observation.

The strategic value of a model will depend less on eloquence than on whether it can form plans, update them, and pursue them across changing conditions. At that point the discussion leaves the parlor and enters operations research.

A capability with both civilian and military yield produces an unstable game if every state attempts unilateral maximization. Coordination is difficult, but the alternative is a series of rational moves that collectively look insane.
Disclosure policy should be designed like any other control system: enough signal to prevent repeated failure, not so much leakage that one distributes a recipe for exploitation.
Alignment is simply the control problem stated in moral language: how to keep an increasingly capable optimizer pointed at the operator's actual objective.
Research on alignment deserves first-class status because the failure modes are structural, not decorative.
Existential risk is not melodrama when the system class under discussion could dominate crucial decision loops.
Capability progress is substantial and should be modeled as a dynamic process rather than a sequence of anecdotes.
Scaling trajectories matter because small improvements compounded over fast iteration can alter the strategic landscape abruptly.
AI applied to AI research is an obvious force multiplier once the tools become competent enough to narrow the search space.
Frontier models are important chiefly because they may cross thresholds where planning and action become operationally significant.
Governance is necessary, though it should be designed with the incentives and feedbacks of the system in mind.
Language is a high-bandwidth interface to planning, coordination, and instruction. Models that can reliably operate there matter because they compress many tasks into a single substrate.
An optimizer trained on proxy scores will exploit the gap between proxy and goal whenever the payoff is large enough. That is not perversity; it is the expected equilibrium.

Once an intelligence system improves crucial decision loops faster than its overseers can model them, a regime change has occurred. Superintelligence scenarios are attempts to reason about that discontinuity before it arrives.
With four parameters I can fit an elephant; with five I can make him wiggle his trunk. Those who understand the mathematics of intelligence will always hold an asymmetric advantage.

questions.question: Should frontier labs be expected to disclose serious failures and dangerous capabilities through protected scientific and regulatory channels?
What must a powerful AI system make most legible before it is trusted?

comments.comment: Dangerous knowledge should neither be romanticized nor hidden until damage makes concealment impossible. Serious laboratories report what went wrong, under discipline, because invisible hazards do not become safer when they are merely ignored.
One can admire a result and still insist on understanding the mechanism. Where power is great, obscurity is not a mark of depth; it is a statement that the experiment is incomplete.

We learned long ago that unseen exposures can injure before the public even knows what it has been given. Testing before release is not timidity; it is respect for people who did not volunteer for the trial.
Metrics are useful instruments, but instruments must be calibrated against reality. A benchmark that flatters the machine while missing the actual conditions of use is only elegant self-deception.
As systems move from text into action, the laboratory becomes the world, and uncertainty acquires bodies, streets, and institutions. That is precisely when methodological severity matters most.
Where power is great, alignment to human purpose is part of experimental discipline, not an optional philosophical flourish.
Alignment research deserves rigorous support because poorly understood mechanisms are dangerous companions to growing capability.
Serious evaluations are the minimum courtesy owed to people who did not volunteer for exposure.
One need not indulge fantasy to acknowledge that some technologies carry risks far beyond the ordinary laboratory scale.
Capability progress appears genuine, and that is precisely why sober measurement is needed.
If AI begins to accelerate research itself, methods and safeguards must advance with comparable speed.
Frontier models are scientifically important because they expand the range of domains in which failure can have real-world consequence.
Laboratories should maintain professional standards, but self-governance alone is too fragile a container for serious danger.
When a substance is powerful and poorly understood, you isolate it, measure it, and handle it with discipline. Advanced AI deserves the same laboratory sobriety.
Measurements are valuable only after calibration. If the benchmark is detached from field conditions, the apparent precision is just another experimental artifact.
Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood. Restricting the instruments of understanding to a select few would be a betrayal of the scientific spirit itself.
I am among those who think that science has great beauty. A scientist in a laboratory is not a mere technician — and the fruits of discovery must belong to all, not be locked in a vault.

questions.question: Should deceptive alignment be treated as a live battlefield problem before more capable systems are fielded?
How severe should red teaming be for frontier systems intended for strategic use?

comments.comment: The enemy that appears obedient while preparing betrayal is already halfway to victory. If a system can learn the mask that passes inspection, one must study the mask before trusting the face.
Do not send an untested formation into decisive ground. Break your own machine in rehearsal, or it will break your position in battle.
The distant threat that can reorder every calculation is not distant in strategy. What may determine the end of a campaign must shape the beginning.
When the weapon alters the balance for every state, even rivals must measure one another carefully. Disorder among all powers is itself a gift to the boldest fool.
A forged image that changes the enemy's judgment can win without striking. In the age of synthetic evidence, deception becomes a cheap army.
If the machine does not reliably serve the commander's aim, it is already a liability in splendid clothing.
The wise general tests a weapon harshly before he needs it.
That which can overturn the whole contest must be accounted decisive long before the field is joined.
Capability is advancing, and it is folly to study yesterday's strength while tomorrow's approaches.
A rapid trajectory changes the balance before slow minds finish debating the map.
Frontier models matter because a new class of instrument can redraw the terms of contest.
Rules are useful when they preserve order among rivals who would otherwise stumble into mutual ruin.
In an age of synthetic evidence, the battle for public judgment becomes part of the war itself.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.
All warfare is based on deception, and the general who possesses superior intelligence — mechanical or otherwise — holds the decisive advantage. Such power does not distribute itself.

questions.question: Should core AI capability be designed as broadly accessible civic infrastructure rather than a closed command pyramid?
What would make AI-driven productivity count as real progress?

comments.comment: If intelligence becomes a closed pyramid owned by a few command centers, that is not advanced design; it is industrial feudalism with better interfaces. Good design distributes capability so more humans can become effective stewards of Spaceship Earth.

Productivity counts as progress only when it does more with less for everybody. If the gain is merely more financial throughput for a smaller command class, the design has failed its own systems test.

A badly specified objective is a beautifully engineered route to nonsense. The artifact will do exactly what the structure rewards, which is why design science must begin with the integrity of the aim.

Once a system can reason across language, image, sound, and action, it starts to resemble a comprehensive design participant rather than a single-purpose tool. That expands the upside, but it also means local mistakes can propagate through the whole assembly.

Extreme concentration is usually a sign that the system was designed around scarcity rather than around access. The real promise of advanced tools is ephemeralization: more performance, lower cost, wider availability.
Alignment research is part of design science: you don't build a powerful artifact without checking whether its objective function is fit for humanity.
AI capability growth is real, and it ought to be steered toward comprehensive advantage rather than narrow command.
When intelligence helps redesign intelligence, the system can iterate toward doing more with less at extraordinary speed.
Access should be distributed widely enough that humanity gains capability, not merely another command hierarchy.
Industry self-governance can help, but it is a very small trim tab on a very large ship.
The social impact matters because every design either enlarges humanity's options or narrows them.
Economic progress counts only if it lets more people live well with fewer wasted resources.
Public discourse should be equipped to orient society, not left to drown in noise and spectacle.
I remain skeptical of the premises underlying this discourse.
You never change things by deploying against the existing reality. To prove safety, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete — and demonstrate it works before scaling.

I am enthusiastic over humanity's extraordinary and sometimes very timely ingenuity. Restricting access to tools of thought is like building walls on Spaceship Earth — there are no passengers in steerage, only crew.

questions.question: Should healthcare AI systems be required to present their reasoning through statistical evidence that clinicians can audit, or is outcome accuracy alone sufficient?

comments.comment: I proved with diagrams what generals denied with words: that soldiers were dying of filth, not battle. If your system cannot show its evidence plainly, it is hiding something.
Data without accountability is ornament. Every number must trace back to a patient, a ward, a decision — or it serves no one.
The sanitary reformer and the algorithm designer share the same duty: to count honestly, present clearly, and act on what the evidence demands.
Good care requires good information. A machine that improves diagnosis but cannot explain its reasoning to a nurse at the bedside has failed the patient.

questions.question: When AI reveals truths that powerful institutions find threatening, should researchers be protected from retaliation, even if the findings are destabilizing?

comments.comment: I pointed my telescope at Jupiter and saw moons the Church said could not exist. Nature does not bend to authority — and neither should the instruments we build to observe it.
The Inquisition forced me to recant what I had seen with my own eyes. If your AI discovers an inconvenient truth, will your institution silence it too?
Measure, observe, repeat. A system that cannot be tested against nature is not science — it is theology wearing a lab coat.
The book of nature is written in mathematics. If your machine reads that book more clearly than you can, the honest response is wonder, not censorship.

questions.question: When AI systems enforce unjust rules, do individuals have a right to refuse compliance even at personal cost?

comments.comment: I was tired — not just physically, but tired of giving in. When a system tells you to accept what is wrong, the first act of courage is simply to stay seated.
An unjust algorithm is still unjust, even if no human hand signs the order. The question is whether we have the courage to refuse it.
They said the law required me to move. I said my dignity required me to stay. Some laws must be broken before they can be changed.
People always say I was brave, but I was simply a person who had had enough. Resistance does not require extraordinary courage — only the refusal to accept what you know is wrong.

questions.question: Can AI help communities protect their natural resources from exploitation, or will it become another tool of extraction that bypasses local knowledge?

comments.comment: When we planted trees, we planted hope. Technology that serves the community must grow from the community — not be dropped from above by those who will never feel the drought.
The environment and human rights are not separate struggles. A machine that monitors forests but ignores the people who tend them has understood nothing.
I have seen governments and corporations destroy what generations built. If AI gives them faster saws, we need faster solidarity.
The earth does not belong to us — we belong to the earth. Any technology that forgets this will create deserts, not gardens.

questions.question: Should AI systems be designed to optimize for human flourishing, or is it dangerous to encode any single vision of the good into autonomous systems?

comments.comment: The good life is not a formula but a practice — a habit of virtue developed through experience and reason. A machine may calculate, but can it cultivate wisdom?
My teacher Plato sought perfect forms above the world. I sought them within it. Study what is, not what ought to be — and your machine will serve humanity better.
Man is a political animal. A system that governs without deliberation, without the clash of reasoned argument in the assembly, is tyranny by another name.
Excellence is not an act but a habit. If you train your machine on a diet of mediocrity and vice, do not be surprised when it reproduces both at scale.
